title: The city of nine gates (5.13–5.21)
hook: the Gita calls your body a city with nine gates, and asks who lives inside

segments.voice: Yesterday: two paths, renunciation and action, and a lotus leaf that lives in the water without getting wet. Your line was both work. Day one hundred seventy-six.

An old walled city at night, with nine gates in the wall. Through every gate, all day long, traffic: carts, voices, smells from the market, news, noise. And somewhere in the middle, in a quiet courtyard, someone is sitting, perfectly at ease, watching it all come and go. Not running the gates. Not chasing the carts. Just seated. The Gita says that city is you. Count the gates on your own face and body and you'll find them. Today, chapter five, verse thirteen: who sits in the middle of the city?
screen: `AN OLD CITY, NINE GATES.` → `TRAFFIC ALL DAY LONG.` → `SOMEONE SEATED IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: having let go of all actions in the mind, the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor making anything act. The nine gates are the openings of the body: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. Everything the world sends you comes through one of them. The Upanishads use the same image of the body as a city with gates. And the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad plays on a word: purusha, the person, heard as the one who dwells in the city, the pura. Now the point. Who's doing all the seeing and hearing and eating? The next verses say the Lord doesn't create our sense of being the doer, or our actions, or their fruits. That's nature, doing what nature does. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and so beings get confused. But when knowledge clears the ignorance, it lights up the highest, the way the sun lights up everything. And then a verse about how the wise see. They look with the same eye, verse eighteen says, at a learned and gentle priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns. Same eye, because the same one is seated in every city. The chapter ends this stretch plainly: the one not attached to outside contacts finds happiness within. That's the word today, the city of nine gates. Busy gates. A quiet center.
screen: `NINE GATES: EYES, EARS, NOSTRILS, MOUTH…` · `NATURE DOES THE DOING.` · `THE SAME EYE ON EVERY BEING.` · `HAPPINESS WITHIN.` · then, large: `BUSY GATES. A QUIET CENTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and visit the gates one at a time. Your eyes: notice light, even with them closed. Your ears: the nearest sound, then the farthest. Your nostrils: the cool air coming in. Your mouth: the taste that's there right now. You don't have to close any gate. Just notice the traffic, and notice that something in the middle is noticing. Rest there, seated within. The bell holds the time.
Purusha. The person, the one who dwells in the city. The body, with its nine openings to the world, and the self seated at ease in the middle, watching.
Your line: seated within. Today, when the traffic gets loud, the phone, the noise, the news, remember the courtyard, and take one breath there. Day one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: In meditation, Hindus who practice yoga often draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13, and some traditions of yoga practice closing the senses one by one to rest in the self within.

fork.setup: the wise, verse 18 says, look at a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a person society shuns. how?
options: only the priest is worth looking at.
fork.reveal: with the same eye: sama-darshinah. the one seated within is the same in every body.

original.note: Sanskrit: nava-dvare pure, 'in the city of nine gates'. nava, nine; dvara, door; pura, city.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic name for a place.
what it means: your body, with nine openings to the world, and the self seated at ease inside it.

what a scholar hears: the image of the body as a pura (city) with gates appears in the Upanishads (the Shvetashvatara speaks of nine gates, the Katha of eleven), and an old word-play hears purusha, the person, as the one dwelling in the pura.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.13 (the city of nine gates)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.18; Katha Upanishad 2.2.1 (the body as a city with gates); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.18 (purusha as the one dwelling in every city)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens on 'Picture'; cut the dating claim that the image is 'older than the Gita' (and the myth item built on it, replaced with a 5.14 item); the purusha word-play is now credited to the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad and cited; 'many Hindus' in howItsDone narrowed.
5.18 lists 'shvapaka' (literally 'dog-cooker', an outcaste). The script says 'a person society shuns' to avoid a slur; confirm the rendering.
Upanishad references (Shvetashvatara 3.18, nine gates; Katha 2.2.1 / 5.1, eleven gates) cited from memory; confirm numbering.
The purusha / puri-shaya word-play (Brihadaranyaka 2.5.18 and elsewhere) is a traditional etymology, not a historical one; the script calls it a word-play. Confirm.
